title: Picnic-band style compared with the band at the Paddock; solos and tempos
summary: Old picnic bands played slower, with little soloing, rested five minutes between numbers, and played to please the dancers, unlike today's club work.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, getting back to the bands at these picnics, there would be six pieces. Yeah, that's right. And there'd be a clarinet, and what else? A clarinet, a tromborong, a trumpet, a bass, a drum, and a band. I understand you. Do they play anything like that? Do they play Dixieland now, would you say?
No. Pretty much. Slower or faster? Well, slower than what we play.
You mean at the paddock? Yeah. At the paddock.
Did they take a lot of solos like at the paddock? No. No.

They took a lot of solos. So there were some differences in them. Yeah, sure. The band just played along. Nobody stood up and took solos. A man might put a take down. A fella take down and he'd have to play a couple of chords and the band just keep on. When he come back up somebody else, take down. That's how they used to play in them games. What about the banjo? Would he ever take a solo? No. Well, not that. No, I don't think. If so, I don't remember. Drum solos then? No. And bass? I don't remember bass or any of those. I was forgetting to be taking solos in them days. Yeah.

So what would happen if one of the horns got tired, he'd take down, then the other two would play? Yeah, let's keep going. The other two would play? Yeah. Would there ever be a time when there was just one horn playing? Like just a trumpet or just a clarinet? Well, I guess so, yeah.
What would he play? Would he play a lead or variations or what? Just the one horn going? Well, that I don't remember. I don't remember.
Would the people applaud for solos like they do at the paddock now, you know, when somebody stands up and takes a solo, and the next fellow stands up and takes a solo?

No, it was just when the dance, when the number was over, people would just stop dancing and say, I don't tell you, play another number. It's pretty hard to applaud. Why are you dancing? It would be about five minutes. The band would rest between the numbers about five minutes. They'd take a blow and then play another number. It was nothing like they do now. Well, you don't ever get tired at the paddock, do you? Oh, I get tired sometimes. Well, how long do you have between numbers there? Well, between numbers there, it seems to me you don't have any time. It seems to me too. Yeah. What's the slowest tempo you ever played at? I mean, during the course of an average night, do you play many slow numbers there? No. What about at a dance? Would you play many slow numbers? Well, at a dance it all depends who you play for. You have to feel the people out and see what they like the best. How do you tell what they like the best? Well, by playing a slow number. Paying attention. I mean, they get on the floor. They play no medium. They play no fast one. Whatever one you see they take to the best, you know, that's what they want. That's what they like the best. So your idea then is to please the public on a dance, right? I think that's the best idea too. I better please the public on a dance. Well, I don't think that always happens on Bourbon Street myself. I don't think they're playing the police the public there a lot of times. Oh, no. I don't think that. They're playing the police the night club on. I don't want to make you say that, but that's what I think.

You know? That's something else. Well, then the bands that you first started playing yourself, did they play like these old picnic bands, or more like the band at the paddock now? No, more so like the picnics bands you should play. In other words, you wouldn't take a lot of solos or anything? No. Would you have any numbers where you featured a special part, a special kind of solo, like on High Society, say? Like that time that was about the home and when they're out and during that?
